files.lesson.md: --- order: 5 unit: angle-sums node: AC9M7M05 n2 title: Angles in a polygon summary: Split a polygon into triangles from one corner. A shape with n sides makes n − 2 triangles, so its angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Stop signs are octagons, honeycomb cells are hexagons, a soccer ball is pentagons and hexagons. The triangle rule tells you the angles of all of them." connection: tiling-shapes app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8163 url: http://127.0.0.1:8163/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: geo.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A pentagon splits into 3 triangles from $A$: $3 \\times 180° = 540°$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@geo.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Split it into triangles" say: "To find a polygon's angle sum, split it into triangles." clip: - caption: { text: "A square's four angles add to 360°.", say: "A square's four angles add to three hundred and sixty." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Split it from A: 2 triangles, 2 × 180° = 360°.", say: "Split it from A: two triangles, two times one eighty." } - click: Split into triangles - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Five sides: 3 triangles, 540°.", say: "Five sides make three triangles: five hundred and forty." } - click: More sides - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Six sides: 4 triangles, 720°. Always two fewer than the sides.", say: "Six sides, four triangles. Always two fewer than the sides." } - click: More sides - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "4 × 180° = 720°" } - wait: 1500 --- You know that the angles of any triangle add to $180°$. A **polygon** is any closed shape with straight sides: a quadrilateral (4 sides), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), octagon (8) and so on. Can the triangle rule tell you the total of a polygon's angles, without measuring a single one? ## Predict: four corners ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a total for a quadrilateral before splitting it makes the board a test of their idea: 4 corners do not mean 4 × something, or 180° again." check: type: predict q: "What do the four angles of a quadrilateral add to?" options: - "$360°$" - "$180°$, like a triangle" - "$540°$" - "It depends on the shape" actual: "360°. Any quadrilateral splits into 2 triangles from one corner, and 2 × 180° = 360°." ``` Think about a square or a rectangle first. Does a lopsided quadrilateral have the same total? ## Run: split a quadrilateral ```step stage: run insight: "Splitting a quadrilateral from one corner shows two triangles whose angles exactly fill the four corners, so the total is 2 × 180° whatever the shape." try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Press **Split into triangles**, then drag the corners into a new quadrilateral. Was your prediction right?", when: "n = 4 and k = 2" } ``` The board measures each angle and adds them up. **Split into triangles** draws lines from corner $A$ to the corners that are not next to it. Drag the corners and watch both totals. ## Investigate: a triangle for each side, less two ```step stage: investigate try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#pentagon", height: 640 } insight: "Lines from one corner split a shape with n sides into n − 2 triangles, and those triangles' angles exactly fill the polygon's corners, so the sum is (n − 2) × 180°. Ben's split adds the angles around his middle point too." tasks: - check: type: trace text: "Split shapes on the board, or in your head, and fill in the table." table: | | sides | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 8 | | triangles from one corner | 1 | [2] | [3] | [4] | [6] | | angle sum (°) | 180 | [360] | [540] | [720] | [1080] | explain: "Each shape makes 2 fewer triangles than it has sides, and each triangle adds 180°." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ben" text: "Ben finds the angle sum of a pentagon. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: polygon-centre-angles explain: "Line 4: his 5 triangles also have angles around the middle point, a full turn of 360°, which are not angles of the pentagon. 900° − 360° = 540°." - check: type: answer q: "What do the angles of a hexagon (6 sides) add to?" answer: "720" feedback: - ["1080", "That is 6 × 180°. From one corner, a hexagon splits into fewer triangles than it has sides."] - ["900", "That is 5 × 180°. How many triangles from one corner?"] explain: "6 − 2 = 4 triangles, and 4 × 180° = 720°." ``` ### Splitting from one corner Here is the method for a pentagon. ```worked \text{A pentagon has 5 corners} :: Choose one corner, $A$. \text{Lines from A to C and to D} :: Join $A$ to every corner that is not next to it. 3 \text{ triangles} :: The two lines split the pentagon into 3 triangles. \text{Their angles fill the pentagon's corners} :: Every triangle's corners are at the pentagon's corners, and together they fill them exactly. 3 \times 180° = 540° :: So the pentagon's angles add to 540°. (n - 2) \times 180° :: A shape with $n$ sides splits into $n - 2$ triangles this way. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Ben's working one line at a time. Which line counts angles that are not the pentagon's? ### A hexagon ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a lopsided pentagon (same total), a corner that points in (still 360°), more sides on the board, then the rule without the board." try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#pentagon", height: 640 } tasks: - starter: "geo.yml#pentagon" hint: "Move any corner. Does the number of triangles change?" check: { type: board, text: "Drag the pentagon into a lopsided shape (keep every corner pointing out). Split it: what is the total?", when: "n = 5 and k = 3", explain: "Still 3 triangles, so still 540°." } - starter: "geo.yml#dart" hint: ["Drag one corner towards the middle of the shape, past the line joining its neighbours.", "Look at the angle at that corner: it is more than 180°."] check: { type: board, text: "Edge case: drag one corner in so it points into the shape. What is the total now?", when: "n = 4 and v = 0", explain: "Still 360°: the corner that points in has a reflex angle (more than 180°), and the other three shrink to make up for it. A shape with a corner like this is concave; one with all corners pointing out is convex." } - starter: "geo.yml#choose" hint: "Use More sides. How many triangles does each new side add?" check: { type: board, text: "Make a polygon whose angles add to $1080°$.", when: "s = 1080", explain: "8 sides: 6 triangles, 6 × 180° = 1080°." } - check: type: answer q: "Without the board: what do the angles of a 12-sided polygon add to?" answer: "1800" feedback: - ["2160", "That is 12 × 180°. From one corner, how many triangles?"] - ["1980", "That is 11 × 180°. A shape with 12 sides makes 12 − 2 triangles."] explain: "(12 − 2) × 180° = 10 × 180° = 1800°." ``` ### A lopsided pentagon Each task changes one thing. First: the same pentagon in a new shape. ### A corner that points in ### More sides ### Twelve sides ## Practise: the rule ```step stage: practise insight: "The rule forwards, for an equal-angled shape, and backwards from a total, mixed; the review keeps the triangle rule fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "What do the angles of a 10-sided polygon add to?" answer: "1440" feedback: - ["1800", "That is 10 × 180°. How many triangles from one corner?"] explain: "(10 − 2) × 180° = 1440°." - check: type: answer q: "A regular hexagon has 6 equal angles. How big is each one?" answer: "120" feedback: - ["720", "720° is the total. Share it between the 6 equal angles."] - ["60", "That is 360° ÷ 6. Find the hexagon's angle sum first."] explain: "The angles add to 720°, so each is 720° ÷ 6 = 120°." - check: type: answer q: "A polygon's angles add to $900°$. How many sides does it have?" answer: "7" feedback: - ["5", "5 is the number of triangles (900 ÷ 180). How many sides make 5 triangles?"] explain: "900° ÷ 180° = 5 triangles, and a shape with 7 sides makes 7 − 2 = 5 triangles." - check: type: question q: "Review: a triangle has angles $35°$ and $75°$, and a third angle. Do the three add to more than, less than, or exactly $180°$?" options: ["Exactly $180°$", "Less than $180°$: $35 + 75 = 110$", "It depends on the third angle"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is only two of the angles. With the third, any triangle's angles add to 180°.", "Whatever the third angle is, the three add to 180°."] explain: "Every triangle's angles add to 180°, so the third angle is 180° − 110° = 70°." ``` ### Ten sides ### Equal angles ### Backwards ### Review ## Make: from a total to a shape ```step stage: make insight: "Building a shape from a given total reverses the lesson: from the angle sum back to the number of triangles and sides." try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#choose", height: 640 } hint: ["How many lots of 180° make 1260°?", "That is the number of triangles. A shape has 2 more sides than triangles."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a polygon whose angles add to $1260°$.", when: "s = 1260", explain: "1260° ÷ 180° = 7 triangles, so 9 sides." } ``` Work it out first, then use **More sides** to check. Stretch: why can no polygon have angles that add to $1000°$? ## Make: tiles that fit, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A tiling needs the angles meeting at a point to add to 360°, so the gap left by three regular pentagons shows why they do not tile." hint: ["Find the angle sum of a pentagon first.", "Angles around a point add to 360°."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Can regular pentagon tiles meet three at a point with no gap? On paper, work out how many degrees are left over at the point when three regular pentagons meet." steps: - ["The angles of a pentagon add to (5 − 2) × 180 = 540°", "a pentagon splits into 3 triangles"] - ["Regular means equal angles, so each is 540 ÷ 5 = 108°", "all five angles match"] - ["Three pentagons use 3 × 108 = 324°, and a full turn is 360°, so 360 − 324 = 36° is left", "angles around a point add to 360°"] - ["A 36° gap is too small for another pentagon (108°), so they do not tile", "the gap must be filled exactly"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Why compare the angles with 360°?" options: - "Tiles meeting at a point must fill the full turn around it" - "A pentagon's angles add to 360°" - "360° is the angle sum of any polygon" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Its angles add to 540°.", "The sum depends on the number of sides."] answer: "36" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["72", "That is the outside angle, 180° − 108°. Add three inside angles and take the total from 360°."] - ["324", "That is what the three pentagons cover. The gap is what is left of 360°."] criteria: - "I found the angle sum and then one angle of the regular pentagon." - "I compared three of them with 360°." - "I said why a gap means no tiling." explain: "Each angle is 540 ÷ 5 = 108°. Three use 324°, leaving 360 − 324 = 36°, too small to fit another pentagon. Regular pentagons leave gaps." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Real tiles also have grout gaps, but the angles decide which shapes can fit. Work down the steps, then type the gap. **Also used in** - **Floors and walls.** Squares and regular hexagons tile because their angles add to 360° at a point. Pentagons leave gaps. - **Honeycomb.** Bees use hexagons, which fill the space with no gaps. ```teacher summary: Students split polygons into triangles from one corner, find that a shape with n sides makes n − 2 triangles, and use (n − 2) × 180° for the angle sum (AC9M7M05, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can split a polygon into triangles from one corner and find its angle sum. - I can explain why a shape with n sides has an angle sum of (n − 2) × 180°. - I can find the number of sides from an angle sum. struggle: Why the angle sum is (n - 2) x 180, not n x 180. Ask students to draw the triangles from one corner and count them. before: > Do the Run board and the Make task yourself first. Students need the last lesson: a triangle's angles add to 180°. The method is to draw lines from one corner only (the board's Split into triangles). Students who split from a point in the middle get n triangles and must take off the full turn of 360° round that point: that is Ben's mistake, planted after the method. The board only splits convex shapes (every corner points out). A concave shape (a corner that points in, with a reflex angle) is the edge case in Modify: the angle sum is still (n − 2) × 180°. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Students who chose 180° are treating every shape like a triangle; '4 × 90°' students may pick 360° for the wrong reason. Ask: does a lopsided quadrilateral still add to 360°?" - "Run: ask students to drag the corners into a very lopsided quadrilateral and read both totals: the measured one and 2 × 180°." - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Draw a pentagon, choose A, draw the two lines at writing pace, shade the 3 triangles, then write 3 × 180° = 540°. Reveal the prepared lines afterwards to compare. Then fill the table together and ask: what is the pattern?" - "Modify: before the 1080° task ask students to predict the number of sides, then use More sides to check." - "Practise: the 'backwards' question plants 5 (the number of triangles). Ask: how many sides make 5 triangles?" - "Make: collect answers and reasons. Then the stretch: 1000 is not a multiple of 180." - "Make on paper: ask what the angles at a point must add to, and why 36 degrees is a problem." stuck: - see: A student counts n triangles (Ben's split from the middle). ask: Which angles in your triangles are not corners of the polygon? fix: "Point at the angles round the middle point: a full turn, 360°. Take it off, or split from a corner instead." - see: A student draws lines from A to the corners next to it. ask: Do those lines make a new triangle? fix: Those lines are sides. Join A only to the corners that are not next to it. - see: A student thinks each angle of any pentagon is 108°. ask: Is the pentagon on the board regular? What happens to one angle when you drag a corner? fix: "108° is each angle of a regular pentagon only: 540° shared equally. The total is 540° for every pentagon." stretch: Why can no polygon have angles adding to 1000°? Each interior angle of a regular polygon with 20 sides? (162°.) support: Use the choose board (More sides) to count triangles for each shape. A printed table with the first two columns filled helps students see the pattern. leads: > Next in class: finding unknown angles in triangles and polygons, giving the angle rule as the reason (node 3). Where it leads: exterior angles (they add to 360° for any convex polygon), which regular polygons tessellate, and the turtle: a closed shape turns 360° in total, which the coding pathway uses for its polygons. exit: q: Find the angle sum of a heptagon (7 sides), and explain your method. a: 900°. From one corner it splits into 7 − 2 = 5 triangles, and 5 × 180° = 900°. explain: > To find the angle sum of a polygon, **split it into triangles from one corner**: draw lines from that corner to every corner that is not next to it. A shape with $n$ sides splits into $n - 2$ triangles, and their angles exactly fill the polygon's corners. So the angle sum is $(n - 2) \times 180°$. A quadrilateral: $2 \times 180° = 360°$. A pentagon: $3 \times 180° = 540°$. A hexagon: $4 \times 180° = 720°$. ```
